title: Own Your Exit
promise: Why cheap leaving keeps a place fair, and how to own what you'd take with you.

cards.text: A restaurant can keep a dress code because you can walk across the street. *House rules stay fair when leaving is cheap.*
On most apps your name, your followers and your posts live inside the app. Leaving means starting from zero, so its house rules start to work like laws.
So own the parts yourself: your name, your connections, your work. Some open networks are built that way, and there an app is just one front door among many.
*A name you control.* An email address on your own domain survives any change of provider. Some social networks let that domain be your handle too.
*Keys you can take back.* Give each app a limited key, never your password, like a valet key that won't open the trunk. Big accounts list the ones you've given.
*Connections and work you sign.* On some open networks every post and follow carries your signature, so any app can show it and anyone can check it.

cards.def: Being able to take the data you gave a service to another one, in a format it can read. In the EU it has been a legal right since 2018 (GDPR, Article 20).

cards.heading: Keeping your number, 2003
cards.text: In 1996 US regulators ordered mobile carriers to let customers keep their numbers when they switched, starting in 1999. The industry called it too costly and won delays. The regulators' reasoning was plain: people stay with a carrier they dislike when leaving costs them their number. A court turned down the carriers' challenge, and in November 2003 numbers began to move. Within a year, more than 8.5 million had.

cards.claim: In 1970 the economist Albert Hirschman, who wrote the classic book on exit, saw a catch: when leaving is too easy, people stop speaking up. Why argue about the dress code when you can cross the street? Then problems go unfixed.
cards.reply: True, and he wrote the other half too: the possibility of exit makes voice work better. Complaints get answered when everyone knows you could go. You don't have to leave the biggest app to keep it in check. It only has to know you can.

cards.text: If the app you use most changed its rules tomorrow, what could you take with you, and what would you leave behind?

cards.prompt: Own one piece of your digital life this week: your name, your connections or your work. Start with the one you'd miss most.
steps: Export it into a folder you control, then open the file to check it's all there.
Open your account settings and take back the keys of apps you no longer use.
Find a login only one company can recover, and add a backup way in that you control.
Trying a run-it-yourself guide? Use a test account, and never paste a recovery phrase anywhere.

sources.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
sources.author: Albert O. Hirschman
sources.note: The classic account of leaving versus speaking up. Easy exit can weaken the habit of voice, yet the possibility of exit makes voice work better.

sources.title: Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media
sources.author: Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jay Graber and others
sources.note: How one open network lets you claim a domain you own as your handle, signs every change to your data, and lets you move hosts without losing your followers.

sources.title: Cellular Telecommunications & Internet Association v. FCC
sources.author: US Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
sources.note: The ruling that let mobile number portability start in November 2003. It quotes the regulator's reasoning: people stay with carriers they dislike when leaving costs them their number.

sources.title: 8.5M customers switch during first year of LNP
sources.author: RCR Wireless News
sources.note: A trade report of the regulator's count after portability's first year: more than 8.5 million people took a phone number to a new carrier.

sources.title: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 20: Right to data portability
sources.author: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.note: The EU law, applied since 25 May 2018, that lets you get the data you gave a service in a machine-readable format and move it to another.
